item.research_question: How does local composition inhomogeneity in body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) alter the rate-controlling mechanism of dislocation motion compared to conventional BCC metals, and does it equalize the mobility of edge and screw dislocations?
item.material_system: Co16.67Fe36.67Ni16.67Ti30 BCC high-entropy alloy (model random solid solution), compared with α-Fe and Fe-5 at. % Al solid solution
item.processing_route: Atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) code; interatomic interactions described by an embedded atom method (EAM) potential by Zhou et al.; dislocation loops (radius 15 nm) created on (11-10) planes; constant shear stress applied in steps of 50 MPa at T = 300 K; minimum energy paths calculated using climbing image nudged elastic band (CINEB) method without external stress
item.test_conditions: Temperature T = 300 K; applied shear stress (τ) ranging from ~250 MPa to ~1 GPa; dislocation loop radius 15 nm on (11-10) slip plane; simulation time ~2.0 ns for velocity estimation
key_findings: In α-Fe at τ ~400 MPa, edge dislocation velocity is 1.8 km/s while screw dislocation velocity is 0.5 km/s, a factor of 3.6 difference.
In Co16.67Fe36.67Ni16.67Ti30 HEA, a stress threshold of 250 to 300 MPa exists below which all dislocations are immobile.
Above the threshold in HEA, edge and screw dislocations move at similar velocities (within a factor of 2) via a jerky, intermittent mechanism.
The activation energy barriers for detrapping in HEA are in the range of 0.1 to 0.4 eV for screw dislocations and 0.1 to 0.3 eV for edge dislocations.
In the high-stress regime (Regime II, τ > 600 MPa), the effective drag coefficient (Beff) is ~1.2 × 10−4 Pa⋅s for edge dislocations and ~1.6 × 10−4 Pa⋅s for screw dislocations in the HEA.
In α-Fe, the drag coefficient (B) for screw dislocations is 2.1 × 10−4 Pa⋅s, which is one order of magnitude larger than that for edge dislocations (2.6 × 10−5 Pa⋅s).
Ti atoms appear to segregate around cross-kinks on screw dislocations and trapping sites for edge dislocations, accentuating local composition fluctuations.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that local composition inhomogeneity in HEAs creates a rugged energy landscape where nanoscale detrapping (NSD) of kinks on screw dislocations and trapped segments of edge dislocations becomes the rate-limiting process. Unlike conventional BCC metals where kink nucleation limits screw mobility, in HEAs kinks nucleate easily but are strongly trapped by locally favorable chemical environments, requiring an activation barrier of ~0.1–0.4 eV to propagate. This NSD mechanism slows edge dislocations significantly, making their mobility comparable to screw dislocations, whereas in conventional BCC metals edge dislocations glide smoothly with negligible barriers.
item.limitations: The simulations cover a short time (2.0 ns) and use empirical EAM potentials that capture general trends but may not represent the exact degree of ruggedness in real-world laboratory HEAs; the specific potential used is an empirical model and not a literal representation of the real-world alloy.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that introducing more local chemical order via prolonged processing or tuning alloying elements could increase activation barriers and stress; they also propose that the mechanisms identified may contribute to pronounced strain hardening and warrant further investigation into dislocation multiplication.
quotes: The activated process becomes nanoscale detrapping, of kinks on screw dislocations and of trapped segments of edge dislocations, presenting an activation barrier of similar magnitude for both dislocation types.

The resultant inhomogeneities, while locally promoting kink nucleation on screw dislocations, trap them against propagation with an appreciable energy barrier, replacing kink nucleation as the rate-limiting mechanism.
The mobility of the screw dislocation is lower than the edge by a factor of 3.6 (0.5 vs. 1.8 km/s) at 300 K.
